title: Rewind & Amplify
text: We are Qubits from Florida Gulf Coast University. We model how hidden defects change quantum measurement patterns, then test a method for querying that model on IBM hardware. Laser diagnosis is a separate research extension.
sources: Original project README and docs/REPORT.md. Event: https://entangledsolutionsgroup.com/Qiskit-Fall-Fest-2026/. Conceptual cover generated with OpenAI image generation.
cue: Nicholas introduces the problem. First nine slides cover the original quantum computation.

title: Hidden defects can change the state before readout
text: Why analyze defects? A hidden two-level system can exchange energy with a qubit or shift its frequency. Then the state evolves differently from the ideal circuit. We infer quantum behavior from repeated preparations and measurements. One readout does not reveal an arbitrary full quantum state. If our analysis ignores hidden dynamics or detector errors, we can assign the wrong cause to the observed statistics. Defect analysis can inform calibration, operating frequencies and device selection, helping preserve useful computation and interpret state estimates. Our project tests a modeling approach to that analysis. It has not diagnosed an unknown physical defect or performed complete state tomography.

title: A click is one recorded measurement outcome
text: A click means the model output reads one in a time step. Zero means no click. This example reads zero, zero, one, zero: a click at step three. Our query selects that step alone and allows any earlier history. Optically, the bit represents a detector firing. On IBM, a superconducting qubit represents that output. The emitter and hidden qubit carry memory to the next step. This repeating model is a quantum recurrent state machine, or QRSM.

title: The QRSM connects each bit to a hidden-state model
text: The QRSM connects each observation to a physical hidden-state model. Each bit conditions the emitter and possible defect state, contributes to the record likelihood, and changes the next prediction. Across records, classical fitting compares coupling and noise settings. A fresh synthetic test shows why this matters. Ignoring detector dead time pushed inferred coupling from a true 0.65 to 0.069. Modeling the blind detector bin moved it to 0.706 and improved prediction on unused records. Other parameters stayed biased. A detector error can otherwise receive a false physical explanation. Classical hidden-state models also capture history, so the quantum structure must earn its value. Our IBM experiment uses a prepared zero state and known model settings. Grover then queries that model; it does not identify an arbitrary unknown state.

title: Hidden memory changes what follows a click
text: This is the useful prediction. Given a click at step three, how likely is another later? Without a hidden defect, the click resets the modeled emitter. A coupled hidden qubit retains memory and changes what follows. At step six, these models predict about ten percent and five percent. History gives a richer test than an overall count. A new IBM follow-up separates the programmed alternatives in one circuit, but keeps substantial bias. Other implementations reverse the contrast. The exact curves explain what the query should return. More accepted shots must also preserve that answer.

title: Rare conditions waste ordinary samples
text: The selected click occurs in 3.95 percent of ideal runs. Ordinary rejection needs about 25 runs for one match, with cost growing as one over its probability. Amplitude amplification reduces coherent model calls to order one over the square root of that probability. That is the quantum rationale, not a wall-clock speedup. Our strongest classical baseline directly samples conditional answers without rejection and wins at this small size. The possible future opportunity is a hidden quantum memory that becomes expensive to represent classically, provided the reversible quantum circuit stays accurate. That crossover remains unproven.

title: A reversible model makes amplification possible
text: Grover must run the model backward, but a reset discards information. We replace each reset with a fresh output qubit and defer measurement. A prepares the histories. The oracle marks the selected condition. A dagger reverses the preparation. A reflection followed by preparation changes interference so matching histories become more likely. We then reduce hardware cost. Steering is classical tuning of a supported event. Local reflection checks fewer qubits but introduces approximation. We verify both event rate and conditional accuracy. Qiskit builds the circuits, Aer checks the exact model, and compiled circuits run on IBM. Amplification is established. Our contribution is this recurrent-model construction and its tested adaptations.

title: Fewer gates, more matching answers
text: We repeated the comparison on IBM Marrakesh with a common initial qubit mapping. In this fresh follow-up, local reflection returned 76.90 percent matching shots, versus 69.26 percent for full reflection. It used 58 rather than 125 native two-qubit gates. The gain is 7.64 percentage points, with a shot-based interval from 6.29 to 8.99. Shorter circuits use fewer scarce operations per accepted answer here. Conditional error is also lower: 0.118 versus 0.181, where zero is ideal. This still leaves bias. Routing and circuit widths differ, and the follow-up was selected after the first run. Suppression did not improve the earlier comparison. Reliable qubits and accurate circuits matter together. We claim this bounded cost-and-quality result, not dollar savings or a classical speedup.

title: The query returns a prediction about the next clicks
text: In the app, we select a click at step three. Switching from plain sampling to full amplification raises acceptance while preserving the predicted future probabilities. Now switch the hidden-memory model to an emitter alone. The step-six probability changes from about five percent to ten percent. That is the answer we wanted: how a candidate hidden interaction changes later observations. These are saved, verified model calculations. The separate IBM data measure circuits representing those models. Neither is a live laser measurement, and amplification does not increase photons from a real source.

title: Quantum-dot source quality and the QRSM
text: Quantum dots connect our question to semiconductor photon sources. Photonic operations rely on predictable interference, which equal brightness cannot guarantee. Engineers need to qualify and tune sources for photonic chips. We now implement a joint-photon observation model: the hidden environment changes emitted modes, and each pair outcome updates its conditional state. Classical calculations verify it, and IBM circuits test its digital representation. The first small-data test barely distinguishes the hypotheses. More controlled data helps, but calibration errors can imitate the signal. No real dot is fitted. Next is our separate frequency-monitoring study.

title: The classical reference leads with unknown onset
text: The test hides when frequency changes and holds out simulated sessions. Can the monitor respond within 32 seconds? The conventional receiver detects 51.35 percent. Adding the atomic channel reaches 58.02 percent, a 6.67 point gain. A second independent conventional reference reaches 97.97 percent. False alarms below refer to the entire 128 second record, not each instant. We include missed events in the delay calculation. Degraded atomic coherence can reverse the benefit, and shared-path drift still mimics the source. These controls sharpen our conclusion: an atomic reference can add information in this model, but the conventional addition performs best. Apparatus resources are not fully matched.

text: Our contribution is a queryable recurrent quantum model with fresh hardware tests and a joint-photon observation extension. Controls changed our conclusions: accuracy and cost both matter. title: Deep optical queries show large distribution errors
text: Both retained three-bin models pass exact branch and conditional-state checks before hardware. Native routing raises these queries to 26,749 and 54,998 CZ gates. Each returns zero selected shots out of 512. That alone is inconclusive: even ideal expected counts are below one. title: Sensor assumptions and resource accounting
text: The atomic response follows finite driven Bloch rotations with T1/T2 damping, preparation error, asymmetric readout error and binomial projection noise. Optical intensity changes the Rabi frequency and induces an assumed light shift during pulses. Conventional receivers include source-photon shot noise, electronics and reference drift. All methods see the same underlying source task and duration. The photon allocation is a declared assumption: atomic coupling and beam geometry are not specified from a real apparatus, and reference lasers plus atomic support optics are not included in a full cost comparison. Therefore this is not a resource-matched quantum advantage test.

title: Detector dead time can distort inferred coupling
text: After a click, the next recorded bit is forced to zero while the underlying system evolves unconditionally. Ignoring that readout process misattributes detector correlation to the hidden interaction. Including it improves held-out log likelihood by 0.4584 nats per 24-bin record, with paired conditional 95% interval 0.3978–0.5210. The fitted coupling moves closer to the known synthetic value, but dephasing reaches its upper bound and efficiency remains biased. A trained HMM captures the detector correlation too: the corrected physical model’s advantage over it is unresolved. Other physical parameters and the family remain known. This fresh result replaces the earlier truth-informed candidate-count example in the current deck.

title: Where the quantum component enters
text: A sensor can use quantum dynamics while a classical computer processes its readouts. We now compile the finite driven atomic channel, including dissipation, into an IBM digital circuit. That tests a bounded implementation on superconducting hardware, not an atom, physical optical coupling or a 128 second acquisition. Unknown-onset detection still runs as classical inference on synthetic records. The separate recurrent-model query uses coherent preparation and amplitude amplification. Connecting a calibrated full acquisition process to a competitive quantum algorithm remains further work. No end-to-end quantum advantage follows from executing a component.

title: The transfer to lithography needs its own test
text: The distinction matters. A CO2 drive laser heats tin to create plasma, which emits EUV. Monitoring the drive is different from measuring EUV. A narrow-line 698 nm atomic benchmark does not automatically transfer to either of those signals or to a 193 nm broadband pulsed excimer source. Existing conventional monitoring measures relevant source quantities. Cymer and imec reported controlled wafer experiments correlating light-source changes with critical-dimension behavior. That motivates source metrology, not a quantitative yield claim for our sensor. Atomic laser-noise metrology is also established prior work, including Bishof and colleagues in 2013.

title: One step of the recurrent quantum model
text: The emitter rotates under a drive. A hidden qubit rotates under its detuning and exchanges excitation with the emitter. The emitter then exchanges with a fresh output qubit. The dynamic implementation measures and resets that output each step. The purified implementation retains it, so the environment and history required for reversal remain in the circuit. This trades extra qubits for reversibility. Model steps are dimensionless. The optical labels describe a model interpretation. These IBM circuits did not measure photon arrivals.

title: Judging rubric and evidence map
text: This map follows the supplied Qiskit Fall Fest judging rubric. Exceptional performance asks for a specific stakeholder and realistic impact, a defensible quantum rationale that considers classical alternatives and hardware scale, reproducible Qiskit implementation, rigorous comparisons, a clear contribution relative to reused ideas, accessible delivery within the time limit, and shared understanding. The hardware bonus is a separate highest-tier item, not an additive sum of all tier values. We do not predict a judge score.

title: Drive amplitude: a useful negative result
text: The field-amplitude proxy is the drive parameter, not an incident-photon flux. A 20 percent field step would correspond to 44 percent intensity under fixed coupling. This low-count regime yields poor timely detection alongside substantial full-record false alarms. The physical filter, fitted HMM and count detector share the same bits; these are not independent engineered optical receivers. The post-holdout prior-only control exposes a weak constant-estimate comparison: for this step, using observations only slightly improves the prior estimate, and for the four other source-changing cases it makes estimation worse. Afterpulsing produces 10.55 percent false source alarms. The model needs a better operating regime and calibrated detector dynamics before a practical monitor claim.

title: Phase inspection: benefit depends on the budget
text: A doubled fringe has a pi ambiguity. Pure NOON performs well locally around a shared calibrated working point, but fails to identify the full phase globally. A charged coherent pilot resolves that ambiguity in the tested hybrid. Both sample modes illuminate the object; the resource is 20,000 mean photons before object transmission, including reference-arm photons. The high-efficiency case has 90 percent object transmission and 90 percent detection, with ideal preparation. Lower transmission removes the precision benefit. At one-percent preparation, matching dose requires 100 times longer for pure NOON; at fixed clock time its precision is worse. Ideal number-resolving detection, a known phase reference and the declared classical protocol bound this result. It is not superiority over all classical designs or a measured feature-size benefit.

title: The full spatial query is costly to construct
text: This is an actual constructed reversible 49-cell oracle, not an extrapolation from three cells. Four count qubits per cell encode a capped Poisson law,23 bits accumulate the weighted score, and 170 extra clean ancillas support explicit reversible gates. title: Exposure: contrast trades against dose and loss
text: The response combines declared linear and two-photon activation coefficients, loss, phase jitter, finite pixel collection and post-activation blur. Activations are rare Poisson events, not direct photon probabilities. The NOON pattern has stronger mean contrast and higher best guard-cell accuracy under the nominal assumptions, but requires more incident photons at its best tested dose. The duty-cycle comparator concentrates equal average photons into ten-percent active time, giving higher peak intensity. It is one explicit classical competitor, not an optimum over all illumination. Loss, blur, linear leakage, background and low preparation success degrade the result. The 20 guard cells exclude boundary cells. This is a sensitivity study of an assumed resist, not a prediction for an available material or fabricated feature.

title: Model accuracy is part of the resource budget
text: The original optical circuit uses only two cavity levels. Comparing its conditional predictions with a six-level reference reveals errors of several percentage points, especially under stronger drive. Increasing the cutoff reduces the discrepancy in these cases, but raises state and circuit costs. Six fresh joint-inference cases fit five parameters with source and detector controls. Fixed settings do not resolve performance versus an HMM; controlled settings give small held-out gains under shared known physics. Fixed-drive detuning sign remains structurally ambiguous. Controlled settings break that exact symmetry but do not establish reliable finite-data sign identification. Local curvature intervals fail near boundaries and are not global uncertainty guarantees. Thermal, multimode and non-Markovian effects remain future model families.
